extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political and social sciences (thinkers on scientific method)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for the proper scientific method in studying social/political phenomena: which modes of reasoning are appropriate or fallacious, how to combine deduction with empirical verification, and how to delimit useful generalizations and subfields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the Chemical Method (single‑cause experimental reductionism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to apply the 'Chemical' or elementary experimental method—isolating a single cause by subtracting the effects of other causes—to social and political phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experimental argument in complex social cases can only verify conclusions drawn from general laws; one cannot subtract the effects of all concurrent causes except one. Insisting on pure experimental isolation would force relying on many separate a priori reasonings (one for each concurrent cause) and is therefore misconceived for social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the Geometrical/Abstract Method (single‑law universalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assimilate the deductive study of society to geometry, where demonstrated truths are universal and unaffected by other principles; social phenomena are not governed by single immutable theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometry has no analogue of conflicting or counteracting causes; in society most phenomena result from many causes whose effects can cancel or modify one another. Treating each social effect as produced by one single property of human nature (as in some geometrical-style political theories) is misleading and unscientific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base theory on unbending practical maxims or abstract rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid deducing political doctrine from asserted practical precepts (abstract right) or assumed original conventions (social contract) as if they were empirical premises for theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using practical maxims as foundational premises is a petitio principii because rules of conduct should be grounded on the theory of the subject, not vice versa. Such an approach treats an art (politics) as if it were a purely deductive science and confuses polemic with scientific theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the Concrete Deductive Method (deduction from many premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat social science as a deductive science like astronomy or mechanics, but deduce from many premises—compound the laws of several causes rather than deducing from one or a few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correct deductive method for sociology infers effects from the laws of the separate elements (laws of human nature) and compounds the tendencies of multiple coexisting causes. Adaptations and precautions are required because compounding many tendencies greatly increases difficulty and precariousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Verification (a posteriori corroboration) as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Always collate deductive conclusions with concrete phenomena or empirical laws; confidence rests on concurrence between a priori deduction and a posteriori observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification is the third essential constituent of the deductive method. In complex cases the order between deduction and verification may be inverted: sometimes provisional conclusions come from specific experience and are afterward connected with human‑nature principles (the inverse method), but the concurrence of both types of evidence is the ground for confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for tendencies rather than precise positive predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that sociology can generally only establish tendencies (what a cause will tend to produce), not exact quantitative predictions of outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the complexity and the multitude of concurrent causes, we can often determine the direction of tendencies but not the extent to which they will operate or whether they will be counteracted. Nevertheless, knowledge of tendencies is valuable for guidance in policy and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the intermixture/consensus of laws (holistic dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always consider that every social phenomenon is influenced, to some degree, by the whole condition of society—there is a 'consensus' among social elements—so isolated analysis is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No social phenomenon is independent; each cause, as its effect spreads, contacts different agencies and is differently modified. Hence general propositions are hypothetical and valid only relative to the full set of circumstances; two societies differing in circumstances will not yield identical results from the same cause without reanalysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit deductive generalizations to phenomena mainly governed by few causes
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid frivolous or worthless generalizations, restrict deductive theorems to classes of social facts that are, in the first resort, principally influenced by a small number of causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the number of concurrent causes in a hypothetical combination grows, uncertainty increases rapidly. Useful general propositions should be confined to those social phenomena where immediate determinants are limited (so that individualizing circumstances can be feasibly taken into account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create distinct branches for different species of social facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate sociological inquiry into distinct but related departments (e.g., Political Economy) when particular phenomena are mainly influenced by a particular class of causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a large class of phenomena chiefly depends on one psychological law or class of outward circumstances (for example, pursuit of wealth), it is expedient to study that class apart, determine effects due to those causes, and then allow for modifying circumstances. This specialization facilitates practical application and repeated use of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reanalyze premises for different societies/times (contextual specificity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume a cause will have the same tendency in different peoples or ages without reexamining the particular circumstances; each case requires its own analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the modifying circumstances differ across societies and periods, a cause that tends one way in one society may have a different tendency elsewhere; thus one must refer back to the premises and perform the analysis afresh for each society or epoch to obtain valid conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of direct deduction and apply the inverse method where needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where direct a priori deduction is inapplicable (due to prodigious complication), use the inverse method: generalize from historical/specific experience and then relate those generalizations to laws of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comte emphasized the inverse order (generalizations from history verified by deduction). The text concedes this has important truth: some inquiries must proceed from empirical laws to theory, while in other cases direct deduction remains applicable. Use the method appropriate to the inquiry's character.
